### **1.  Introduction & Executive Summary** 

#### **

1.1 Introduction** At the time of our previous Quarterly report (beginning of September), the extent of the debt crisis within the Eurozone was not clear. Earlier in the year, the crisis had focused on Ireland and Portugal with concerns also being raised about Greece. Now, however, the concerns have spread to larger economies such as Italy and Spain, and even other major economies are being ensnared in the net. The copper market has not been immune to such developments. The cash quote hit a year-to-date low of $6,722/tonne in October, down 34% on the February high, and average prices for that month fell to a 14-month low of $7,348/tonne. Although further moves below the $7,000/tonne level have since been avoided, current price levels remain some way off the $9,000/tonne-plus averages that were seen for seven out of the first eight months of the year, when the focus of the market was very much on the tight supply-side fundamentals rather than broader economic concerns. In terms of demand, consumption had held up relatively well until recently despite the deteriorating economic climate. However, producers have, over recent months, confirmed the slowdown in demand. This view is supported by the limited statistics that are available on copper semis output - in China, Italy, Japan and the United States - as well as by a dip in physical premiums. As discussed in Section 1.4, the worsening economic outlook has also led to more cautious positioning from investment funds. In terms of supportive factors, output continues to “come in” below expectations. Such is the myriad nature of these disruptions that we assume that they will remain a feature of the market going forward. As a result, despite a notable downgrade to our demand projections, we continue to expect that the market will post a notable deficit this year, of 372,000 tonnes. Despite this, exchange inventories have fallen only slightly this year, largely due to the decline on the Shanghai Futures Exchange. The discrepancy is, in large part, accounted for by the decline in unreported stocks within China over the first three quarters of the year; such trends are certainly in line with the information that we received on our recent field research trips to the country. Importantly, the extent of this Chinese destocking has slowed, and is believed to have gone into reverse over the fourth quarter, as a weakening of LME prices led to a surge in imports and a concurrent decline in LME inventories over October and November (the latter can be clearly seen in the chart on page 4). This renewed buying activity has, along with ongoing supply disruptions, served to provide some degree of support to prices from the early-October low. Implicitly, although we are bullish on copper’s medium-long term prospects, our economic assumptions (outlined below and discussed in detail in Chapter 2), point to only limited price upside over the near term. #### **1.2 Economic Assumptions** Since our previous Three Year Copper Forecast published in September, demand prospects for the base metals complex have deteriorated. Although this has been perhaps surprisingly slow to filter through to a significant decline in consumption of copper cathode, Thomson Reuters GFMS expects that the demand environment will deteriorate further over the next six months. Importantly, the easing of growth rates is not just coming from the debt-stricken Eurozone, but also from many of the leading copper consuming countries. Trends in our favoured broad-based indicator – the OECD composite leading indicator – are still pointing to weaker demand conditions. The indicator fell to 100.1 in October, representing the eighth successive decline. The slowdown in the Eurozone is having “knock on” effects on most other regions. Importantly, all the key groupings within the broader index – BRICs, Eurozone, Japan and NAFTA – were either flat or lower on a month-on-month basis. No one individual economy is immune from this trend, but obviously some economies are better placed than others to cope with the slowdown. **Base Case Scenario** (with a 45% probability outcome): Real global GDP growth is expected to ease to 2.8% this year, having rebounded to 5.1% in 2010. This is due to the indebted position of both governments and consumers in much of the developed world and the impact of monetary policy tightening in emerging markets.

Next year, we forecast a further decline in world GDP growth to an average of 2.5%, due to deterioration in the European sovereign debt situation.  This is then followed by faster growth rates in 2013 and 2014 as the more traditional sources of growth, such as consumer spending and the property market, start to improve. 

Given ongoing concerns about underlying economic growth, we expect US GDP growth to slow to 1.2% in 2012 before economic conditions improve from 2013 onwards. 

We would expect further austerity measures to be enacted in the Eurozone; which in turn will continue to reduce the region’s growth.  Real GDP growth is therefore forecast to fall to 0.9% in 2012 with a possibility of outright contraction in some quarters before a gradual recovery takes place in the final two years of the forecast. 

The prospects for Japanese growth are constrained by the yen’s persistent strength and weakening external demand.  GDP is expected to grow by 1.6% in 2012, with only modest growth rates for the remainder of the forecast period. 

China’s economic growth slowed to an annualised 9.1% in the third quarter, down from 9.5% in the previous quarter.  Nevertheless, we expect China’s economy to expand by at least 9.0% this year since the economy should benefit from continued policy efforts to raise

**Scenario B** (with a 40% probability outcome): Under our most bullish view of the world economy, we expect a rapid recovery in confidence. Central to this scenario are policies implemented by the US government and the Federal Reserve, including fiscal stimuli and further quantitative easing.  We also expect the ECB to start more aggressive monetary easing, which is already starting to emerge.  In addition, developing countries’ export sectors are expected to benefit from the stronger GDP growth in the developed world.  Moreover, amid the inflationary environment and a lack of withdrawal of monetary stimulus, we expect to see the US dollar weakening through to 2013. 

**Scenario C** (with a 15% probability outcome): Under our low case scenario, we expect sluggish growth rates, particularly in the developed world, together with very low levels of inflation.  World GDP growth is therefore projected to average around 2.3% over the forecast period.  Although growth rates generally improve towards the end of the forecast, they remain at historically low levels, especially for a post-recession phase of economic growth.

However, weak export markets will ensure that even developing markets will grow at a slower rate than under the Base Case. #### **1.3 The Dollar** The US dollar started to regain strength against the euro since September. This was mainly driven by a poor economic performance in Europe and its ongoing sovereign debt crisis. Overall, amid increased uncertainty and turmoil in the financial markets the dollar’s appeal as a safe haven asset has been rising, boosting its value against all major currencies. Looking further ahead, we believe that the measures adopted by Eurozone countries so far will not be sufficient to resolve the crisis. As a result, we expect the dollar to regain strength against the euro over the forecast period. Furthermore, as US interest rates start rising from 2013 onwards, we expect the dollar to strengthen against most currencies. As such, we expect that over the next three years an average exchange rate of $1.28/€ would represent a fair equilibrium. This takes into account purchasing power parity and the United States having a similar inflation rate to the Eurozone. #### **1.4 Investment** We are beginning to see the other side of the coin in terms of the impact on the LME-traded metals. The bulk of the investment interest in base metals tends to be focused on the copper market. As we have discussed on a number of occasions, investment funds are by no means a homogeneous group. However, in the current environment most participants are adopting a much more cautious approach to the sector. The actions of the trend-following funds are fairly straightforward. As copper prices have fallen through various support levels, they have established essentially negative signals in terms of chart patterns, moving averages and other technical indicators. Other investment funds have increasingly viewed the base metals complex as a vehicle to invest in global economic growth and in particular to participate in the rapid metals-intensive growth underway in China and the other BRICs. Copper has benefited more than the other metals given that, historically, it has attracted the greatest amount of investment interest and, along with aluminium, has much better liquidity than the other base metals. **5** Three Year Copper Forecast - December 2011 **CONFIDENTIAL** Investor Positions in

Another attraction for investment activity in copper has been its superior fundamentals compared to the other metals, particularly aluminium, which again has boosted investment fund interest. Within the investment community there are also commodity specific funds, which closely track the fundamentals of the individual metals; again copper had been, during the early part of the year, a beneficiary of the positive positioning from this sector. In the current economic and financial environment there has been an increase in risk aversion, and this has seen a change in attitude towards cyclical assets such as copper. This trend may continue in the coming months and we have not seen much buying on dips at this stage. However, when the global economy picks up, we expect that copper will remain the metal of choice for investment funds. At the moment, the timing of the re-emergence of a long-side bias is unclear, and we may see some short positioning over the near term. #### **1.5 Consumption** The outlook for global consumption growth has weakened markedly since the release of our previous Quarterly Three Year Copper Forecast, amidst growing concerns over the health of the global economy. This is being aggravated by the worsening European debt crisis. After estimated growth of around 6.0% over the opening six months of the year, we expect copper usage to grow by just 2.0% year-on-year over the second half as a slowdown in Chinese demand growth is exacerbated by contracting mature economy consumption. For 2011 as a whole, Thomson Reuters GFMS expects global copper usage to grow by 3.9%, revised down from the 5.4% growth forecast in our previous report. Looking ahead to next year, we expect global demand growth to slow to 2.7%. In the mature economies, the continued imposition of austerity measures in indebted nations, and the subsequent weakness in economic growth, is set to result in the group’s consumption contracting for a second successive year. This is despite a projected recovery in Japanese demand, facilitated by post-earthquake reconstruction efforts. Elsewhere, slowing growth across the BRIC nations will also serve to constrain the increase in global copper usage. Further forward, we see a slight acceleration in global consumption growth in 2013, to 3.4%, on a brightening economic outlook, before settling

back to 3.2% in the final year of our forecast period. Although we expect mature economy demand to return to positive territory over these years as the macroeconomic environment improves, growth rates will remain relatively constrained and, as such, the BRICs will continue to remain the key driver behind the growth in the global total over the final two years of the forecast. Indeed, although underlying consumption growth is expected to continue to slow across the BRICs, in part due to the high base effect, growth will continue to remain considerable in tonnage terms. Importantly in this regard, we expect that the Chinese economy will experience a soft landing, resulting in copper usage in the world’s largest consumer continuing to grow at a robust (albeit slowing) pace going forward. #### **1.6 Production** The overall picture of the supply-side of the copper market remains largely unchanged from our last Three Year Quarterly Forecast. The tightness at the concentrate stage has continued to persist, as global output continues to be troubled by a variety of factors, including strike action and lower ore grades. This, combined with lower than expected output from SXEW operations, in part due to technical problems, has constrained global mine production growth to just 0.3% year-on-year over the first eight months of 2011. Although prices remain above the marginal cost of production, some of the above-mentioned factors remain in place. As a result, Thomson Reuters GFMS is forecasting global production to remain flat this year, at 15.95 million tonnes, down from our previous forecast which showed growth of 3%. The underperformance of recent years, coupled with the expectation that a number of projects will rampup and others come online, has led us to forecast a noticeable acceleration in output next year. However, it must be noted that even our forecast of 5.8% in 2012 is considerably lower than the ICSG’s estimate of 9.4%, which largely reflects our conservative projections particularly towards those countries that have underachieved in the past. In the final two years of the forecast period, we expect production growth of 5.4% and 6.3%, respectively, bringing the total to 18.9 million tonnes, 18.3% up on this year’s total. Implicit in these two years is the fact that some of the projects that we expected would come on stream by the end of 2011 and in 2012 will only be realised in the final two years of our forecast. ###### **Global Consumption - y-o-y Change**

Nevertheless, the inability of prices to sustain a downward break has relieved pressure for any price-related cutbacks, so far. The important feature to note is the steep tail of the copper production cost curve, and prices may have to fall significantly, and for a prolonged period, from levels seen in mid-December for producers to cutback in any meaningful way. As such, we are forecasting global refined production to increase by just 2.7% to 19.547 million tonnes this year, down from our last estimate of 4%. However, over the 2012-2014 forecast period, we expect some acceleration in the rate of growth of refined production. Unlike in previous years, the growth should be more broad-based across SX-EW, primary and secondary. Mine production (including SX-EW) should increase by 18% from end 2011 to 2014. Our projected increase to refined output in this period is lower at 13%. This reflects a moderate rebuild of concentrate stocks and a slowdown in the rate of growth of secondary output. Thomson Reuters GFMS forecasts average annual production growth of around 4% between 2012 and 2014. This should take global refined output to 22.023 million tonnes in 2014 from 2011’s estimated level of 19.547 million tonnes. #### Alternative Scenarios Given that prices prior to the New Year are languishing around $7,300-$7,500/tonne, our base case forecasts may seem fairly bullish. However, it should be remembered that just over three months ago in early September, prices were briefly above $9,000/tonne. The most likely factor to push prices towards our high case Scenario B is a quicker than expected revival in demand. Although sovereign debt remains a key hurdle, we are in a phase of low interest rates and some inflationary pressures are beginning to ease. In addition, this scenario assumes that supply continues be below initial expectations, which has been a regular occurrence in recent years. Under these more benign conditions the stock drawdown would be larger than under our base case and would take reported stocks to below one week of consumption. A recent feature has been the shift in investor sentiment away from pro-cyclical assets such as commodities, which has seen both LME metals and related equities decline sharply. The scenario above would see a swift return of investment interest. This, combined with an exceptionally tight fundamental supply picture, could see average prices close to, or above, $10,000/tonne in some years. There has been a modest increase to European refined output so far this year, which has come from a number of sources.  Output continues to be built up at the 72,000 tpy Las Cruces operation in Spain, although primary output in the country is down on year-earlier levels.  Swedish output is up as Boliden lifts capacity at its Ronnskarr plant.  Operating rates have been lifted at KGHM, while higher secondary output has also made a modest contribution.  These factors could lift output by around 150,000 tonnes by 2014 to 3.85 million tonnes. 

In Zambia, the key to future production levels is partly a question of utilisation rates, as there is plenty of spare capacity.
